sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. PV is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled by a date; EV the budgeted cost of the work actually completed; AC the total spent to date. SV = EV - PV and CV = EV - AC (negative: behind schedule, over budget); SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC, below 1.0 meaning behind schedule and over cost for the work done.

sources.cite: Construction Contracting: Business and Legal Principles (Virginia Tech Publishing, open textbook), chapter 22 Construction Contract Claims
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. A change order is usually the owner's action (a directed scope change); a claim is 'a written demand or assertion by the Contractor seeking an adjustment in Contract Price', often after a proposal is denied. Written notice is required within the contract's period; the contractor's submittal must establish entitlement under the contract and quantum (the amount of money or time), a time claim usually by a CPM schedule analysis; the owner accepts, denies or partly accepts, and the contractor accepts or invokes the contract's dispute resolution procedure.

The budget, the weekly planned value, the progress each event costs or recovers, the contingency figure and the trust gauges are teaching figures for exam practice, not measured values. The clinic, the contractor and the people are fictional.

brief.situation: You are the project manager for Lakeshore Family Clinic, a fictional clinic, on the fit-out of its second floor: four exam rooms, a procedure room and a staff room. Brightwater Builders, a fictional general contractor, holds the fixed-price construction contract. The project is predictive: an 8-week baselined schedule from Monday 1 March 2027 and a budget of $240,000, with a $10,000 contingency reserve for the risks in the register.
handover: Sponsor: Dr. Elena Ruiz, clinic director. Contractor's site lead: Sam Okafor. The clinic staff will work in the rooms.
Planned value is $30,000 a week. You get status figures at each Friday status meeting (the kickoff is the first); the dashboard shows PV, EV, AC, SPI and CPI.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the objective and baseline, the work packages, earned value against plan, risks and issues, the people and the milestones.
Move the project on a week at a time. Decisions come to you as they arise; between them you can review the risk register or work out the variances.
At handover you close the project and write a short close-out note.

sinkPrompt.title: End of week 2: the sponsor asks for a second sink in each exam room
sinkPrompt.context: Dr. Ruiz, the clinic director and sponsor, walked the site with Brightwater's site lead: "Infection control wants a second sink in every exam room. It's small; just add them while the walls are open." The site lead looks at you. The plumbing rough-in is on the critical path next week.

choices.label: Log a change request: have Brightwater price it and say what it does to the schedule, then take it to the change control board (Dr. Ruiz and you) to decide

effects.log: Change request CR-03 logged. Brightwater's impact analysis: $8,000 and about a week on the critical path. The board defers the sinks to the summer shutdown; the baseline stands.

choices.feedback: Execute the change control process: a request is analyzed for its impact and decided by those with the authority before anyone does the work.

choices.label: Tell the site lead to go ahead; it is the sponsor asking, and it is small

effects.log: The plumbers start on sinks nobody priced or scheduled.

choices.feedback: Work added outside change control is scope creep: unpriced, unscheduled and outside the baseline, even when the sponsor asks.

choices.label: Tell Dr. Ruiz that no changes are possible once construction has started

effects.log: Dr. Ruiz is told no without an analysis; the request goes nowhere.

choices.feedback: Refusing without analysis is not change control either: a request is assessed and decided, and it may well be approved.

panelPrompt.title: End of week 4: risk R4's trigger has been reached
panelPrompt.context: The register's trigger for R4 was 'no confirmed panel delivery date by the end of week 4'. The supplier still has not confirmed. Brightwater: "They usually come through. We could wait a week, or I can put an overtime electrical crew on now."

choices.label: Execute R4's planned response: order from the pre-approved alternate supplier, drawing about $3,000 from the contingency reserve, and record the change in the register

effects.log: Alternate supplier confirms delivery Wednesday of week 5. Register updated: R4 closed, residual risk (fit of the alternate panel) noted.

choices.feedback: The trigger fired, so the planned contingency response is executed and its residual risk recorded.

choices.label: Wait a week for the usual supplier to confirm

effects.log: The risk becomes an issue: the panel arrives two weeks late.

choices.feedback: Waiting past the trigger lets the risk become an issue on the critical path.

choices.label: Add an overtime electrical crew now, without going back to the plan or the sponsor

effects.log: Overtime crew booked: $18,000 not in the plan, and the panel is still late.

choices.feedback: Crashing spends money on the wrong problem: the constraint is the panel, not labor, and the planned response was cheaper.

reportPrompt.title: End of week 5: the monthly status report
reportPrompt.context: PV ${pv}k, EV ${round(ev)}k, AC ${round(ac)}k (SPI {spi|2dp}, CPI {cpi|2dp}). Brightwater's site lead: "Just put green on it; we'll catch up." Dr. Ruiz reads the report before the board meeting on Monday.

choices.label: Report the variances as measured, the cause (the clinic's late drawings{risk == "wait" ? " and the late panel" : ""}), the forecast and a recovery plan: overlap ceilings and flooring with wiring in rooms already inspected

effects.log: Report sent with the figures and the recovery plan; Dr. Ruiz approves the overlap.

choices.feedback: Status is communicated as measured, with variance analysis, a forecast and the corrective action.

choices.label: Report green: the budget is fine and the schedule will catch up

effects.log: The report says green while the project is behind.

choices.feedback: A status that hides a measured variance misleads the sponsor and leaves no time to correct it.

choices.label: Report that the contractor is running late, without the figures

effects.log: The report blames Brightwater for a delay the clinic caused.

choices.feedback: The variance has a measured size and a cause; here the cause was the owner's late drawings, not the contractor.

claimPrompt.title: Week 7: the contractor's notice of claim
claimPrompt.context: Brightwater: "Under clause 15 we give notice of a claim for $9,000: extended site costs for the six days the clinic held the equipment drawings in week 3." The contract gives the owner 3 working days to return drawings. Dr. Ruiz: "Can we just sign it so they keep working?"

choices.label: Treat it as a claim: check the notice against clause 15, ask for the substantiation (the transmittal dates, daily logs and a schedule analysis), and negotiate under the contract's dispute steps

effects.log: The records show 3 days of owner delay, not 6. Agreed at $4,500 and recorded as a settled claim.

choices.feedback: A claim is the contractor's demand for an adjustment; entitlement and amount are established from the contract and the records before it is settled.

choices.label: Sign it in full as a change order now, to keep the peace

effects.log: $9,000 signed without review; half of it was not owed.

choices.feedback: A change order is not how a disputed claim is settled, and paying without substantiation pays for delay the owner did not cause.

choices.label: Reject it outright: delay is the contractor's problem

effects.log: Brightwater invokes the dispute clause; the site lead stops volunteering information.

choices.feedback: The clinic did return the drawings late; rejecting a claim without assessing it pushes it toward a formal dispute.

reflection.question: Write the close-out note for the sponsor: where the schedule stood against the baseline and why, and how the change request, the risk trigger and the contractor's claim were handled.

parts.label: Schedule and status
parts.criteria: Reads SPI and CPI correctly (below 1 is behind or over), names the cause of the variance, and says how it was reported and corrected.
parts.modelAnswer: At week 5 SPI was 0.90: behind, because the clinic returned the equipment drawings late; CPI was about 0.97. We reported the figures and overlapped finishes with wiring, and finished on the baseline.

parts.label: Change, risk and claim
parts.criteria: The sinks went through change control; R4's contingency was executed when its trigger fired; the claim was assessed against the contract and the records, not signed or rejected unread.
parts.modelAnswer: The sinks went to the change control board, which deferred them with the impact in hand. When R4's trigger passed we ordered from the alternate supplier as planned. Brightwater's claim was a claim, not a change order: the records showed 3 days of owner delay and we settled for that.

expertPath.text: Log the sinks as a change request, get the impact analysis and let the change control board decide.
R4's trigger has passed: execute its contingency, the alternate supplier, from the reserve, and update the register.
Report SPI and CPI as measured, the cause and a recovery plan (fast-track finishes in inspected rooms).
Treat the notice as a claim: check it against the contract and the records, and settle what is owed.
Close with the clinic's sign-off, lessons learned and the records archived.

onBaseline.headline: Good: on the baseline, under control
onBaseline.body: Every change went through control, the risk response ran on its trigger, the status was honest and the claim was settled on the record.

partly.headline: Delivered, with gaps
partly.body: The rooms opened, but the criteria below show where a change, a risk, the report or the claim slipped out of control.

misreported.headline: Status misreported
misreported.body: A green report over a measured variance took away the sponsor's chance to act. Report SPI and CPI as measured, with the cause and a plan.

overrun.headline: Beyond the harm line
overrun.body: Schedule or cost performance fell below 0.85. Waiting past a risk trigger and work outside change control are the usual ways there.

broken.headline: A working relationship broke
broken.body: Rejecting a claim unread, or refusing the sponsor without analysis, damages the relationships a fit-out depends on.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: The project was not closed before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Planned value is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled, earned value the budgeted cost of the work done, actual cost what was spent; SPI = EV / PV and CPI = EV / AC, below 1 meaning behind schedule or over cost. A request from the sponsor is a change request: analyze its impact and let the change control board decide before anyone does the work. When a risk's trigger fires, execute its planned response and record the residual risk. Report variances as measured, with the cause, a forecast and a corrective action. A contractor's claim is assessed against the contract's notice and claims clause and the project records for entitlement and amount, then settled or taken through the dispute steps.
